newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market entering holiday zone.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market entering holiday zone.

text.p: It is about that time of the year to break out the caffeine pills or drink a lot of coffee as bond market activity is expected to dwindle substantially.
With all the key economic news for November out of the way, and with no more Treasury auctions to bid on, the U.S. Treasury market should start becoming a ghost-town beginning on Friday.
"It is going to be a real snoozer," said a senior trader at a primary dealer.
Adding to the siesta mood, trading desks will be thinly staffed, as players start their Christmas vacation early.
The highlight of the session comes at the end of Friday, when the Federal Reserve releases the minutes from the November Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

"The tone of the minutes might tell us how the Fed sees things at present," said David Greenlaw, money market economist at Morgan Stanley & Co, noting that any reaction to the minutes would likely start in overseas trading on Monday.
"If (the Fed) removed the tightening bias, people might move back their forecasts as to when the Fed might be tightening," Greenlaw said.

Traders said that removing the bias would be bullish for the market, but analysts do not think it was lifted as of yet -- especially as Fed chief Alan Greenspan recently warned of getting too complacent on inflation.

The market, though, seems content -- for now -- that the economy and inflation are under control. Data released on Thursday show evidence of a weakening labor market, as jobless claims were revised higher and manufacturing activity in the Philadelphia Fed region decelerated in early December.
That prompted a surge in Treasury prices, with the 30-year bond jumping 1-1/2 points to 98-28/32 to yield 6.59 percent.
Market participants are not sure if the current levels will hold, since thin trading environments can lead to sharp price swings, and one large trade can virtually move the market.

"Those who wanted to sell have come in already and those who wanted to buy had their opportunities, since they recently had cheaper prices," said Mead Briggs, director of proprietary and government trading at CS First Boston Corp.
Briggs added that despite the potential for "zippy" and "nutty" price action, it would not indicate a shift in sentiment. "People are comfortable" with their positions, he said.

The lone piece of economic news due on Friday is the final revision to third quarter gross domestic product at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. GDP is expected to have grown at a 2.0 percent pace in the third quarter, which would be unchanged from the prior revision, according to a Reuters poll of economists.
GDP "is old news, but it gets people looking at how the fourth quarter is shaping up," Greenlaw said.
He added that the market should continue to follow holiday shopping sales figures.

Late Thursday, the two-year note was 99-28/32, up 5/32, to yield 5.82 percent. The when-issued five year note was at 6.11 percent, down from the 6.165 percent level it was sold at Thursday. The 10-year note was up 31/32 to 101-7/32, to yield 6.33 percent.
